TAQ55.title: Sparks
TAQ55.brief: A good spark effect is not one emitter but several that work together. An emitter is the part of a Niagara system that creates one kind of particle. Here you combine three: soft smoke, a bright flash at the center, and fast sparks that fly out, fall and bounce. In this quest you build a system with these three emitters. Epic's tutorial page uses materials from the Starter Content, which current engine versions no longer include, so you use the default sprite material of Niagara.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Start with the smoke: right-click in the Content Browser, choose FX, then Niagara System, pick New system from selected emitters and add the Simple Sprite Burst template. Name the system SparksSystem, rename the emitter to FX_Sparks_Smoke, and drag the system into a level. If you already have a smoke emitter asset of your own, you can add that emitter to the system instead. Keep the default sprite material, which is a soft round dot.

In FX_Sparks_Smoke, find Emitter State and set Life Cycle Mode to System. Delete Spawn Burst Instantaneous and add a Spawn Rate module with the value 20. In Initialize Particle, make the lifetime random from 2 to 3, make the color dark gray (0.3), and set the sprite size to a random value from 75 to 200. Add an Add Velocity module that points mostly upward, with Z from 25 to 35, and a Shape Location module with a sphere of radius 5.

In the Particle Update group of the smoke emitter, open Scale Color. Turn off Scale RGB, and give Scale Alpha the Smooth Ramp Down shape so the smoke fades out. Add an Acceleration Force module and set it to Z 20.

Add a second emitter from the Simple Sprite Burst template and name it FX_SparkBurst. Delete Sprite Burst Instantaneous, set Life Cycle Mode to System, add a Spawn Rate of 50, set Lifetime to 0.2, and set the RGB of Scale Color to 2, 6, 25. This is the bright flash at the center.

Add a third Simple Sprite Burst emitter and name it FX_Sparks_Radial. In its Sprite Renderer, set Alignment to Velocity Aligned, so each spark points the way it moves. Use a Spawn Rate of 500, a random lifetime from 0.2 to 0.7, a small sprite size, and Add Velocity with a random range where Z goes from 300 to 500.

In the Particle Update group of FX_Sparks_Radial, add Gravity Force with Z -4500, Drag with 1.7, and Collision with Restitution 0.4 and Friction 0.2. Remove Scale Color, and add Scale Sprite Size by Speed with a Velocity Threshold of 2000.
Look at the effect in the level and adjust one value that you do not like, for example the gravity or the spawn rate of the radial emitter.
TAQ55.done_when: Send one screenshot of the Niagara System Overview that shows all three emitters (FX_Sparks_Smoke, FX_SparkBurst and FX_Sparks_Radial). Also send one screenshot of the effect in the level with sparks bouncing on the floor.

quiz.q: Why does the tutorial start the smoke part of the sparks effect from a copy of FX_Smoke instead of a template?
choices: Templates cannot be used twice in one project
Systems and emitters are independent, so you can build a system from an emitter you already made
A copy runs on the GPU and a template does not
Only copied emitters can use the M_smoke_subUV material
quiz.explain: Emitters and systems are separate assets. Epic recommends building systems from existing emitters or templates, so a copy of FX_Smoke is a quick start.

quiz.q: The radial sparks should look like thin lines that follow their direction of movement. Which renderer setting does the tutorial change for this?
choices: Sub Image Size to 8 by 8
Sort Mode to View Depth
Alignment to Velocity Aligned
Material to M_Spark
quiz.explain: In the Sprite Renderer of FX_Sparks_Radial the Alignment is set to Velocity Aligned, so the sprites line up with the particle velocity.

quiz.q: Which two modules make the radial sparks fall fast and slow down in the air?
choices: Acceleration Force and Curl Noise Force
Gravity Force (Z -4500) and Drag (1.7)
Point Attraction Force and Vortex Force
Scale Velocity and Kill Particles
quiz.explain: The tutorial adds Gravity Force with Z set to -4500 and a Drag module set to 1.7 in Particle Update of the radial emitter.

quiz.q: Sparks that hit the floor should bounce back. Which module and setting control how strong the bounce is?
choices: Collision module, Restitution value
Solve Forces and Velocity, Bounce value
Shape Location, Sphere Radius
Emitter State, Loop Behavior
quiz.explain: The Collision module handles hits with the world. Under Bounce, Restitution (0.4 in the tutorial) sets how much energy the bounce keeps.

quiz.q: The Simple Sprite Burst template has Life Cycle Mode set to Self. Why does the tutorial change it to System?
choices: Self mode only works for mesh particles
The system then calculates the life cycle, which usually optimizes performance
Self mode disables the Spawn Rate module
System mode is required for Velocity Aligned sprites
quiz.explain: System mode lets the system calculate life cycle settings, which usually optimizes performance. By default the system loops forever every 5 seconds.

quiz.q: The fast radial sparks should stretch when they move fast. Which module does the tutorial add for this after removing Scale Color?
choices: Scale Sprite Size by Speed
Sprite Rotation Rate
SubUV Animation
Scale Color by Speed
quiz.explain: Scale Sprite Size by Speed scales the sprite by particle speed. The tutorial sets a Y range of 3 to 6 and a Velocity Threshold of 2000.

TAQ56.title: Sprite smoke
TAQ56.brief: A sprite is a flat 2D image that always turns to face the camera, and it is the most common kind of particle. A sprite sheet is one texture that holds many small images in a grid, and playing them one after the other makes the particle look animated. Niagara is the visual effects system of Unreal, and an emitter is the part of a Niagara System that creates particles. In this quest you build a steady column of smoke from sprites. Epic's tutorial page uses a smoke sprite sheet from the Starter Content, which current engine versions no longer include, so you make a simple smoke material yourself.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Make a folder for the effect, for example NiagaraFX/SpriteEffect. In it, create a material named M_SmokeSoft. Set its Blend Mode to Translucent and its Shading Model to Unlit. Add a Particle Color node and a RadialGradientExponential node. Connect the color of Particle Color to Emissive Color, and multiply the gradient by the alpha of Particle Color and connect the result to Opacity. This gives a soft round puff that the emitter can tint and fade.

Right-click in the Content Browser and choose FX, then Niagara System. Pick New system from selected emitters and add the Simple Sprite Burst template. Name the system SmokeSystem and rename the emitter to FX_Smoke.

In the Sprite Renderer, set the material to M_SmokeSoft. Then drag SmokeSystem into a level. If you have a smoke sprite sheet of your own, with for example 8 by 8 images, use a material with that texture instead, set Sub Image Size to 8 by 8 so that the renderer knows how many images are in the sheet, and turn on Sub UV Blending.

In Emitter Update, delete Spawn Burst Instantaneous, add a Spawn Rate module and set it to 50, so the smoke comes out all the time and not in one burst. In Emitter State, set Life Cycle Mode to Self and Loop Behavior to Infinite.

In Initialize Particle, set a random lifetime (2 to 3), a gray color, a random uniform sprite size (75 to 200) and a random sprite rotation (Direct Normalized Angle, 0.25 to 0.5). Add an Add Velocity module with a random range (Z 50 to 200). Add a Shape Location module that uses a sphere with a radius of 64.

In Particle Update, add an Acceleration Force module with Z set to 500 so the smoke keeps rising, and keep Scale Color so that the smoke fades out. If you use a sprite sheet, also add a SubUV Animation module, which plays the images of the sheet one after the other: set its mode to Linear, Start Frame to 0 and End Frame to 63 for a sheet of 8 by 8 images.
Click the Gear icon on the emitter and choose Create Asset From This, so that FX_Smoke becomes its own emitter asset that you can use again. Save everything.
TAQ56.done_when: Send a screenshot of the Niagara Editor with the FX_Smoke stack open, where Spawn Rate and Acceleration Force are visible, and a screenshot of the smoke column in the level. Also show the FX_Smoke emitter asset in the Content Browser.

quiz.q: What is a sprite in Niagara?
choices: A 2D plane that always faces the camera and shows a texture or material
A small static mesh
A light that follows a particle
A sound attached to a particle
quiz.explain: Sprites are 2D camera-facing planes. The renderer draws a texture or material on them.

quiz.q: Why does the tutorial set Sub Image Size to X 8, Y 8 in the Sprite Renderer?
choices: It makes each sprite 8 times bigger
The smoke material of the tutorial is a sprite sheet, so the renderer must know how many images are in the grid
It limits the emitter to 8 particles
It sets the number of LODs
quiz.explain: A sprite sheet holds many images in a grid. Sub Image Size tells the Sprite Renderer how many images there are in each direction, here 8 by 8.

quiz.q: The tutorial deletes Spawn Burst Instantaneous and adds Spawn Rate. What is the reason?
choices: Spawn Burst only works on the GPU
Spawn Rate is needed for SubUV materials
The goal is a constant column of smoke, not one burst
Spawn Burst cannot be used with Shape Location
quiz.explain: A burst spawns everything at once. Spawn Rate (50 per second here) gives a steady column of smoke.

quiz.q: Without the SubUV Animation module, what happens to the smoke sprite sheet?
choices: The particles are invisible
All 64 images show at the same time
The material turns black
The renderer only shows the first image of the sheet
quiz.explain: If nothing plays the sheet, the renderer uses only the first sprite. SubUV Animation with Linear mode from frame 0 to 63 plays all 64 images.

quiz.q: Which module makes the smoke rise over time, and in which group is it?
choices: Add Velocity in Particle Spawn
Acceleration Force in Particle Update
Spawn Rate in Emitter Update
Shape Location in Particle Spawn
quiz.explain: Add Velocity only gives a start push. Acceleration Force (Z 500) in Particle Update keeps pushing the smoke up every frame.

quiz.q: How do you save the FX_Smoke emitter so other systems can reuse it?
choices: Right-click the system and choose Export
Drag the emitter into the level
Click the Gear icon on the emitter and choose Create Asset From This
Save the level
quiz.explain: The Emitter Settings menu (Gear icon) has Create Asset From This, which makes an independent Niagara Emitter asset.

TAQ57.title: Steam
TAQ57.brief: You do not have to build every effect from zero. If you start from an emitter that already works and change a few values, you get a new effect in much less time. In this quest you take a simple smoke emitter and change its speed, color, size and forces until it looks like steam.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. You need a smoke emitter to start from. If you have a smoke emitter asset of your own, right-click it, choose Duplicate Emitter, and rename the copy FX_Steam. If not, right-click in the Content Browser, choose FX, then Niagara System, pick New system from selected emitters, add the Simple Sprite Burst template, and rename the emitter to FX_Steam. In this emitter, delete Spawn Burst Instantaneous and add a Spawn Rate module, an Add Velocity module, a Shape Location module with a sphere, and an Acceleration Force module.

If you started from an emitter asset, right-click FX_Steam and choose Create Niagara System, which makes a new system that already contains the emitter. Name the system Steam and drag it into a level.
In Emitter Update, find Emitter State and set Life Cycle Mode to System. Then set Spawn Rate to 30.

In Initialize Particle, set the lifetime range to 3 to 7, the color to white (1, 1, 1) and the sprite size to 100 to 200. Set Add Velocity so that it pushes the particles sideways and up (X 16 to 32, Y -5 to 5, Z 35 to 50). Set the sphere radius to 20.

In Particle Update, give Acceleration Force a random range with a minimum of X 25, Y -10, Z 15 and a maximum of X 55, Y 10, Z 25. In Scale Color, pick the Pulse Out curve shape, which makes the steam fade in and then fade out.
Add a Drag module, which slows the particles down. When the 'unmet dependencies' error appears, click Fix Issue so that Niagara moves the module to the correct place. Set Drag to 0.8.
TAQ57.done_when: Send a screenshot of the Steam system in a level next to a prop (for example a cylinder that stands for a pipe or a cup), and a screenshot of the Particle Update group that shows Acceleration Force, Scale Color and Drag in the correct order.

quiz.q: What is the fastest way to get a system that contains an emitter asset you already have?
choices: Right-click the emitter and choose Create Niagara System
Drag the emitter into the level
Open Project Settings > Niagara
Rename the emitter with the System prefix
quiz.explain: Right-click on the emitter asset and pick Create Niagara System. The new system already contains that emitter.

quiz.q: Why does the steam drift sideways instead of going straight up?
choices: The sphere radius is 20
Add Velocity and Acceleration Force both have positive X values
Life Cycle Mode is set to System
Scale Color uses Pulse Out
quiz.explain: Add Velocity uses X 16 to 32 and Acceleration Force uses X 25 to 55, so the particles move along X as well as up.

quiz.q: You add Drag and see 'The module has unmet dependencies'. What happened and what do you click?
choices: Drag needs a GPU emitter; click Convert
Drag needs a material; click Assign
Drag is not allowed in Particle Update; click Remove
Drag was added below Solve Forces and Velocity; click Fix Issue to move it
quiz.explain: New modules go to the bottom of the group, after Solve Forces and Velocity. Fix Issue moves Drag above it so the force is solved.

quiz.q: Which curve shape does the tutorial use in Scale Color for steam?
choices: Smooth Ramp Down
Ramp Up Down
Pulse Out
Linear Up
quiz.explain: Scale Color gets the Pulse Out template, so the steam fades in and out over its life.

quiz.q: Compared with the smoke emitter it was copied from, how does steam get a longer life?
choices: Spawn Rate is raised to 30
Lifetime minimum and maximum are set to 3 and 7 in Initialize Particle
Drag is set to 0.8
Life Cycle Mode is set to System
quiz.explain: The lifetime range is changed in Initialize Particle to 3 to 7 seconds, longer than the smoke range.

quiz.q: What does the Drag module do to the steam particles?
choices: It slows them down
It makes them bigger
It changes their color
It spawns more of them
quiz.explain: Drag applies a slowing force. With 0.8 the steam loses speed as it rises.

TAQ58.title: A beam
TAQ58.brief: A beam is a line of particles that are joined together and drawn as one long strip, called a ribbon. Lasers, lightning and tesla coils are all made this way. In this quest you build a beam from a template and add fast, random movement to it so that it looks like flickering lightning.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Create a Niagara System from the Static Beam template. Name it BeamSystem, rename the emitter to FX_Beam and drag the system into a level.
In the Render group, keep the Ribbon Renderer with DefaultRibbonMaterial. In its Tessellation section, set Curve Tension to 0.5.

In Emitter Update, give Loop Duration a Random Ranged Float from 0.1 to 0.2. In Beam Emitter Setup, enable Absolute Start and Absolute End and turn on Use Beam Tangents (both tangents point up in Z). Set Spawn Burst Instantaneous to 35.
In Particle Spawn, set Lifetime to 0.2 so the beam appears and disappears quickly. Keep the Spawn Beam module as it is. In Beam Width, choose the Ramp Up Down curve and set Scale Curve to 5.

In Particle Update, add a Jitter Position module, which moves the particles by small random amounts. Then add an Update Beam module and drag it above Jitter Position. Set Jitter Delay to -0.01 and Jitter Amount to 15.

Optional: on Beam End, make a New Dynamic Scratch Input with an Actor Component Interface, and turn it into a user parameter named Beam_End. Then place a sphere in the level, name it Sphere_BeamEnd, select the system in the level and pick the sphere as the Source Actor, so the beam ends at that sphere.
TAQ58.done_when: Send a screenshot of the lightning beam in the level and a screenshot of the Particle Update group that shows Update Beam above Jitter Position. If you did the optional step, also show the Override Parameters section with Sphere_BeamEnd.

quiz.q: Which renderer draws a beam in Niagara?
choices: Sprite Renderer
Mesh Renderer
Ribbon Renderer with beam modules
Light Renderer
quiz.explain: A beam is a ribbon. The Ribbon Renderer is used together with beam-specific modules such as Beam Emitter Setup.

quiz.q: What do you set in the Spawn Beam module?
choices: The beam color
Nothing, it only needs to be present
The number of beams
The material
quiz.explain: Spawn Beam is the second beam-specific module. The tutorial says you do not need to change anything, it just has to be in the stack.

quiz.q: Why is the particle Lifetime set to a short 0.2?
choices: To save memory
Because ribbons cannot live longer
To make the beam wider
So the beam flickers like lightning
quiz.explain: A short lifetime makes the beam appear and disappear quickly, which looks like flickering lightning.

quiz.q: You added Jitter Position but the beam does not crackle. What is missing?
choices: A Light Renderer
An Update Beam module placed above Jitter Position
A higher Spawn Rate
A Collision module
quiz.explain: Jitter Position needs an Update Beam module, and Update Beam must sit above Jitter Position in the Particle Update stack.

quiz.q: Which renderer setting changes how spiky the lightning looks?
choices: Curve Tension under Tessellation
Sub Image Size
Sort Mode
Facing Mode
quiz.explain: Curve Tension (0.5 in the tutorial) is in the Tessellation section of the Ribbon Renderer and controls how spiky the beam is.

quiz.q: How do you make the beam end follow an actor in the level without Blueprints?
choices: Type the actor name in Beam End
Use a Scratch Pad dynamic input with an Actor Component Interface, expose it as a user parameter and set the Source Actor in Override Parameters
Set Life Cycle Mode to System
Attach the actor to the Niagara component
quiz.explain: The tutorial builds a scratch input that reads an actor transform, turns it into a user parameter (Beam_End), and picks the Source Actor in the Details panel.

TAQ59.title: GPU sprites, thousands of them
TAQ59.brief: Normally the CPU, the main processor of the computer, calculates how particles move. When an effect needs many thousands of particles, this becomes too slow, so you move the work to the GPU, the graphics card. A GPU emitter has one extra rule: you must give it fixed bounds, a box that tells the engine how large the effect is. In this quest you build a swirling ball of thousands of small sprites that runs on the GPU.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Create a Niagara System from the Simple Sprite Burst template. Name it GPUSprite, rename the emitter to FX_GPUSprite and drag the system into a level.
Open Emitter Settings, then Emitter Properties, and set Sim Target to GPUComputeSim so the particles are calculated on the graphics card. Tick Fixed Bounds to clear the warning that appears.
In Emitter Update, set Life Cycle Mode to System. Set the Spawn Burst Instantaneous count to 2500, and add a Spawn Rate module set to 500.
In Initialize Particle, set Lifetime to 5 and Sprite Size to 5 by 5. Then add a Sphere Location module, which spawns the particles inside a sphere shape.

In Particle Update, add a Scale Sprite Size module and set it to Non-Uniform. For Scale Factor choose Vector2D from Float, then choose Float from Curve and pick the Ramp Up Down shape, so each particle grows and then shrinks.

Add a Curl Noise Force module (Noise Strength 72, Noise Frequency 0.02), which makes the particles swirl. Add a Point Attraction Force module (Attraction Strength 5.5, Attraction Radius 300, Falloff Exponent 0.6, Kill Radius 4 enabled), which pulls the particles toward one point.
Add a Color module and set it to Color from Curve. Build a gradient with at least four color stops, and make the alpha (the opacity) fade to 0 at the end.
TAQ59.done_when: Send a screenshot of Emitter Properties that shows Sim Target set to GPUComputeSim and Fixed Bounds ticked, plus a screenshot of the swirling particle ball in the level.

quiz.q: Where do you switch an emitter from CPU to GPU simulation?
choices: Render group > Sprite Renderer
Emitter Settings > Emitter Properties > Sim Target
Project Settings > Niagara
Particle Update > Solve Forces and Velocity
quiz.explain: Sim Target in Emitter Properties is set to GPUComputeSim to run the simulation on the GPU.

quiz.q: Why must you set Fixed Bounds for a GPU emitter?
choices: The GPU has no memory for bounds
Fixed Bounds enables the Spawn Rate module
Fixed Bounds sets the particle color
The system cannot read how big the effect is when the simulation runs on the GPU
quiz.explain: With GPU simulation the system cannot read back the size of the effect, so you give it fixed bounds on the emitter or the system.

quiz.q: What is the difference between Spawn Burst Instantaneous and Spawn Rate in this effect?
choices: Burst is GPU only, Rate is CPU only
Burst makes 2500 particles at once at time 0, Rate makes a continuous 500 per second after that
They do the same thing
Rate is used only for ribbons
quiz.explain: The burst gives a big group of particles at start. Spawn Rate then keeps a stream of 500 per second while the emitter is active.

quiz.q: In Curl Noise Force, what happens when you lower Noise Frequency?
choices: The sphere of particles gets more warped
The particles turn red
Fewer particles spawn
The particles stop moving
quiz.explain: The tutorial says the smaller the Noise Frequency, the more the sphere of particle locations becomes warped.

quiz.q: What does Kill Radius do in Point Attraction Force?
choices: It sets where particles are removed at the end of their life
It sets the spawn sphere size
It sets the color curve length
It sets how many particles the GPU can hold
quiz.explain: Kill Radius is the area where particles dissolve at the end of their life cycle. The tutorial sets it to 4.

quiz.q: When is a GPU sprite emitter the right choice?
choices: Always, it is faster in every case
Only for ribbon effects
When you need tens of thousands of particles and the CPU would struggle
Only when the effect uses collision
quiz.explain: The guide is for effects that need tens of thousands of particles, where CPU simulation can cause performance problems.

TAQ60.title: Particles that cast light
TAQ60.brief: Particles can do more than show an image: each one can also carry a small light that shines on the floor and walls around it. This makes fire, magic and sparks look like a real part of the scene. In Niagara you do this with a Light Renderer, which you add next to the normal Sprite Renderer. In this quest you build a blue fountain of particles that lights up a dark corner of a level.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Create a Niagara System from the Fountain template. Name it ParticleLights, rename the emitter to FX_ParticleLight and drag the system into a dark part of a level. If the level has no dark place, build a small closed room from cubes.
In Emitter Update, set Life Cycle Mode to System and set Spawn Rate to 500.

In Initialize Particle, set a random lifetime (1.75 to 2.5), set the color to R 0.1, G 0.3, B 50, and set a random uniform sprite size (2.5 to 8). A color value above 1 makes the particles glow. Set the Sphere Location radius to 15.
In the Add Velocity in Cone module, set Velocity Strength to a random range of 300 to 600.
Keep Gravity Force and Drag at their default values. Add a Collision module so the particles do not fall through the floor, and click Fix Issue when the error appears.
In the Render group, add a Light Renderer, which creates a light for each particle. Set Radius Scale to 5 and set Color Add to X 0, Y 0, Z 15, which gives a strong blue light.
TAQ60.done_when: Send a screenshot of the fountain in a dark area with blue light visible on the floor and walls, and a screenshot of the Render group that shows both the Sprite Renderer and the Light Renderer.

quiz.q: The tutorial sets the particle Blue value to 50. What does a color value above 1 do?
choices: It makes the color emissive, so the particles glow
It is clamped back to 1
It turns the particle into a mesh
It makes the particle transparent
quiz.explain: The color picker normally works from 0 to 1. A value above 1 becomes emissive color, so the particles glow.

quiz.q: How do you make the particles cast light on the scene?
choices: Turn on Cast Shadows in the Sprite Renderer
Add a Light Renderer in the Render group
Set Life Cycle Mode to System
Add a Point Light actor to the level
quiz.explain: Click the Plus sign in the Render group and pick Light Renderer. It spawns a light with each particle.

quiz.q: What does Radius Scale on the Light Renderer control?
choices: How many lights spawn
The sprite size
How far from the particle the light spreads
The color of the light
quiz.explain: Radius Scale (5 in the tutorial) sets how far the light reaches from the particle position.

quiz.q: The Light Renderer Color Add fields are labeled X, Y and Z. What do they mean?
choices: Position of the light
Red, Green and Blue
Radius, falloff and intensity
Start, middle and end time
quiz.explain: X, Y and Z map to R, G and B. Setting Z to 15 gives a strong blue light that matches the particle color.

quiz.q: Why does the tutorial add a Collision module to the fountain?
choices: Without it the particles fall through the floor
Without it the light does not render
Collision is required for the Fountain template
Collision makes particles spawn faster
quiz.explain: Without collision the particles fall through the floor and other solid objects. The module is moved with Fix Issue after adding.

quiz.q: In Add Velocity in Cone, where is the point of the cone?
choices: At the camera
At the level origin
At the end of the particle life
At the particle spawn point
quiz.explain: The point of the cone is the spawn point. The X, Y and Z values choose the direction the cone opens.
